title: Radiators and Undertow
premise: Elodie Crane, a translator whose childhood language is dissolving word by word, discovers behind her late grandmother's wardrobe a box of letters never delivered — love letters written by the man Elodie believed was merely a lodger, addressed to a woman who was not her grandmother. As she translates them back into the dying tongue of her girlhood, she realizes the final letter contains a confession that rewrites who she is and whom she owes her loyalty to. Delivering it means betraying the family that raised her; withholding it means letting a living man die without the truth. In the end, Elodie reads the sentence aloud at his deathbed in a language only he still remembers — choosing truth over duty, and losing the last of her mother tongue as the price.
about_author: Odile Lockridge spent a decade working as a literary translator in port cities before turning to fiction, and her prose carries the salt-stain of borrowed vocabularies and half-remembered lullabies. She writes from a narrow flat above a laundromat, where she keeps an inventory notebook of every word she has forgotten.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Clearing her grandmother's flat after the funeral, Elodie catalogs the objects she cannot name in her mother tongue anymore, mourning each lost word like a small death. Behind the wardrobe she finds a tin box: forty-one letters, sealed, undelivered, written in a hand she almost recognizes. The emotional beat is quiet grief curdling into unease as she reads the first line and understands these were never meant for her grandmother.

chapters.title: A Man Made of Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Elodie and Tomas, the letters' author, now eighty-three and fading in a care home across town. Elodie tracks him down under the pretense of translation work; he mistakes her for someone else — for the woman the letters were written to. Rising tension builds as Elodie realizes the affair predates her birth, that her grandmother stole these letters to keep a secret, and that Tomas's memory is dissolving faster than her vocabulary.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, climax. The final letter contains one sentence Elodie cannot render into English — not for lack of skill, but because its meaning indicts her own existence: Tomas claims her mother was his daughter. Her family's whole architecture of duty and silence rests on the letter staying buried. Confronted by her uncle, who demands she burn the box, Elodie must choose between the loyalty she was raised on and the truth she was trained to carry across languages. She chooses truth.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV with a closing passage in Tomas's voice. At his deathbed, Elodie reads the final letter aloud in their shared childhood language — the last fluent sentences she will ever speak in it. He answers with the untranslatable sentence, finally translated not into words but into forgiveness. The resolution lands softly: some truths cost everything and give back only a single clear moment, and Elodie leaves the home lighter, her inventory notebook finally empty.
